## Short version

A TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small CPU cache of virtual-to-physical address translations. On a big-memory server, frequent misses each cost several extra memory reads. Huge pages reduce the misses, with new risks in latency and memory use.

## Words used here

- **Page**: the unit of memory mapping. The default size on x86-64 is 4 KiB.
- **Virtual address**: the address that a program uses.
- **Physical address**: the real location in RAM.
- **Page table**: a tree in memory that maps virtual pages to physical pages.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table to find one translation.
- **Page fault**: the kernel's work when a program first touches a page.
- **Huge page**: a page of 2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64.
- **THP (transparent huge pages)**: the Linux kernel uses huge pages without a request from the program.
- **hugetlbfs**: a pool of huge pages that the administrator reserves. Programs must ask for them.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)**: each CPU socket has its own local memory.

## 1. What a TLB is

Every memory access uses a virtual address. The CPU must translate it to a physical address first. The TLB keeps recent translations, one entry per page.

```
virtual address --> [ TLB ] --hit--> physical address
                       |
                      miss
                       v
                 [ page walk ] --> new TLB entry --> retry
```

- **Hit**: the translation is in the TLB. No page table read is needed.
- **Miss**: the CPU does a page walk. That is up to 4 memory reads with 4-level tables [Ref1]. It is up to 5 reads with 5-level tables.

The TLB is small. An example is a recent Intel server core, with 2048 second-level entries [Ref2].

Insufficient data: I do not know the entry counts of your server. The `cpuid` tool prints them.

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

Six effects combine. The example server has 512 GiB of RAM.

- **Small reach.** 2048 entries of 4 KiB cover 8 MiB. The server has 65,536 times more memory than that.
- **Large page tables.** 4 KiB pages need 1 GiB of last-level tables for 512 GiB. The CPU caches cannot hold that. So a walk often reads RAM, about 100 ns est. (300 cycles at 3 GHz).
- **Waiting instructions.** The load cannot finish before the walk ends. Every instruction that needs the loaded value waits too.
- **Cache displacement.** A walk brings page table entries into the data caches. They displace application data.
- **Virtual machines.** Inside a virtual machine, a walk goes through two sets of tables. The worst case is 24 memory reads instead of 4 [Ref3].
- **NUMA.** The page tables can sit in the memory of another socket. Then each walk read takes longer.

The cost is highest for random access across a large data set. A sequential scan misses less often. Each page serves many accesses in a row.

CPUs also cache the upper levels of the table. This often leaves only the last-level read.

## 3. How huge pages help

A huge page lets one TLB entry cover 2 MiB or 1 GiB. The walk also stops one or two levels earlier.

```
4 KiB page:  L4 -> L3 -> L2 -> L1 -> data    4 table reads
2 MiB page:  L4 -> L3 -> L2 -------> data    3 table reads
1 GiB page:  L4 -> L3 -------------> data    2 table reads
```

L4 to L1 are the four levels of the page table.

| Page size | 2048 entries cover | Last-level tables for 512 GiB |
|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 8 MiB | 1 GiB |
| 2 MiB | 4 GiB | 2 MiB |
| 1 GiB | often fewer entries, see section 4 | 4 KiB |

- **Larger reach.** One 2 MiB entry covers 512 times more memory than one 4 KiB entry.
- **Shorter walk.** Each miss needs one or two fewer table reads.
- **Smaller tables.** The last-level tables shrink from 1 GiB to 2 MiB. They fit in the CPU cache.
- **Fewer page faults.** One fault maps 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB.

Linux offers two ways to get huge pages [Ref4] [Ref5].

| Aspect | THP | hugetlbfs |
|---|---|---|
| Who asks | the kernel decides, no code change | the program asks explicitly |
| Page sizes | 2 MiB | 2 MiB and 1 GiB |
| Guarantee | none, 4 KiB pages are used on failure | guaranteed after the reservation |
| Idle memory | returns to the system | stays reserved |
| Can be swapped | yes | no |

## 4. What can go wrong

**THP**

- **Stalls at allocation.** The kernel may compact memory (moving pages to free a 2 MiB block) during a page fault. The faulting thread waits for that. The `defrag` setting controls this behaviour [Ref4].
- **Slower first touch.** The kernel clears 2 MiB per fault instead of 4 KiB. So each single fault takes longer.
- **More memory use.** A touch of 1 byte puts a full 2 MiB into RAM. Sparse data then needs more RAM than before. That can end in out-of-memory kills.
- **Silent 4 KiB pages.** Fragmented free memory makes the kernel use 4 KiB pages without any error. So results differ between a fresh boot and a long uptime.
- **Silent splitting.** A system call that changes part of a huge page splits it into 4 KiB pages. A partial `munmap` is one example. Memory allocators do this when they free memory.
- **Background merging.** khugepaged (the kernel thread that merges 4 KiB pages) uses CPU time. A merge also locks the address space of the process for a short time.
- **fork.** After `fork` (the process-copy call), a write to a shared huge page copies 2 MiB or splits it. The kernel version decides which. Redis documents stalls from this [Ref6].

**hugetlbfs**

- **Reserved memory is unavailable to others.** The pool cannot serve file cache or normal allocations, even when idle. A pool that is too large causes out-of-memory kills.
- **Partial reservation.** A request at run time can return fewer pages than asked, without an error. Reserve at boot. Then read `HugePages_Total` to confirm [Ref5].
- **Wrong NUMA node.** The pool is divided across nodes. The node that runs the program may hold too few pages.
- **Empty pool.** `mmap` fails when the pool is empty. In some cases the process instead gets SIGBUS (a fatal signal) at first touch [Ref5].
- **Few 1 GiB entries.** Some CPUs have very few TLB entries for 1 GiB pages. A program that touches many 1 GiB regions can then miss often.
- **Code change.** The program must ask for these pages explicitly.

**Both**

- **System-wide settings.** The THP mode and the pool size apply to the whole machine. On a shared server, they change other users' results too. The THP mode `madvise` limits THP to programs that ask for it [Ref4].
- **No gain.** A workload with few TLB misses gains nothing. Measure before the change.

## 5. Checks to propose in the review

- **Walk cost before the change.** `perf stat -e cycles,dtlb_load_misses.walk_active` shows the share of cycles spent in page walks. These are Intel event names.
- **THP in use.** `AnonHugePages` in `/proc/meminfo` shows the amount of memory in transparent huge pages.
- **THP failures.** `thp_fault_fallback` in `/proc/vmstat` counts faults that got 4 KiB pages. `compact_stall` counts faults that waited for compaction.
- **Pool state.** `HugePages_Total` and `HugePages_Free` in `/proc/meminfo` show the pool.
